query: How can route-quality factors (sidewalk width, slope, curb ramps, shade, benches) be quantified and transformed into time penalties or comfort-weight weights?

response.query: How can route-quality factors (sidewalk width, slope, curb ramps, shade, benches) be quantified and transformed into time penalties or comfort-weight weights?
response.answer: Route-quality factors can be quantified using ADA standards, then converted into time penalties or comfort weights based on deviation from optimal design criteria. Sidewalk width, slope, and curb ramp design directly impact pedestrian usability and can be weighted accordingly.

results.content: # 642.9 Sidewalk Ramp and Curb Ramp Design Criteria. * 1 642.9.1 Slope and Rise of Sidewalk Ramps. When the running slope, or grade, of a sidewalk exceeds 5% it is a ramp. If the sidewalk is adjacent to the street or separated by a narrow planting strip, the sidewalk grade may be equal to the grade of the street and not be considered a ramp. The cross slope for all ramps is to be 1%, but a maximum of 2.0% is allowed by ADA standards. Although the maximum running slope of a ramp in new construction is 1V:12H (8.33%), as discussed before, all sidewalks are to be designed with the least running slope possible. A landing will be located at the top and bottom of all ramps and between segments that have a 30 in. The landing will be at least the width of the ramp with a minimum length of 60 in.

results.title: 642.8 Sidewalk Design Criteria - Engineering Policy Guide
results.content:
Title: 642.8 Sidewalk Design Criteria - Engineering Policy Guide
| FHWA's *Designing Sidewalks and Trails for Access*: Part I Part II | |. A sidewalk is designed to meet a variety of characteristics that have a direct impact on usability, such as grade, cross slope, width, surface type, etc. Sidewalk design criteria are based on providing access to all pedestrian users to the maximum extent feasible. Sidewalks are not to be designated on paved shoulders located behind a mountable curb; nor shall paved shoulders be designated or striped as a pedestrian pathway, however if pedestrian use is anticipated, efforts should be made to meet ADA standards wherever possible, such as a 2% cross slope. Sidewalks are to be at least 5 ft. However, if necessary due to geometric constraints, the width of the sidewalk may be reduced to 4 ft. There are exceptions: sidewalk width may be reduced to meet site constraints; however, ADA requires a minimum width of 4 ft. This will include repairs and upgrades to existing sidewalks so the facilities provide a continuous minimum width of 4 ft. The width of the accessible sidewalk route should meet the requirements above. Obstructions are objects within the pedestrian access route that reduce the clearance width, protrude into the circulation route, or limit the vertical passage space or of a sidewalk. are not to reduce the sidewalk width to less than 3 ft. ## 642.8.3 Sidewalk Surfaces. The grade of a sidewalk should be as level as possible allowing easy use by travelers. For pedestrian facilities on public access routes, the running grade of sidewalks will be a maximum of 5%. If the sidewalk cannot be kept at the same grade as the adjacent roadway and the grade is greater than 5%, the sidewalk may be considered a ramp and designed in accordance with EPG 642.2 Sidewalk Ramp and Curb Ramp Design Criteria. Sidewalks with a cross slope greater than 2% are noncompliant and must be made compliant by whatever means necessary and including replacement. For more information on the use of landings in ramp design refer to EPG 642.2.1 Slope and Rise of Sidewalk Ramps.
